explanations.explanation: Not even close, friend. The singer says, "My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD…" (Psalm 84:2). That is not a man checking his watch and saying he's in no hurry. Fainting is a whole other level of wanting.

Yes, friend. He says, "My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD; my heart and my flesh cry out for the living God." (Psalm 84:2). Nobody who faints from wanting something says "no rush." This man's whole self is calling out.

That's it, friend. The swallow found a nest "…where she places her young near Your altars…" (Psalm 84:3). A mama bird picked her spot, and she picked it right next to the altars. I think she knew what she was doing.

Close to the nest, but not what the verse says. The swallow has a nest for herself, "…where she places her young near Your altars…" (Psalm 84:3). Food never comes up in that line. It's the little ones who get settled in.
Ha, a swallow with a treasure chest. I would pay to see that. But the verse says she places her young near the altars (Psalm 84:3). Treasures never come up in that line, only her little ones.

Right on the money, friend. The singer says, "How blessed are those who dwell in Your house! They are ever praising You." (Psalm 84:4). Ever praising means it doesn't stop. I wish my mixer had that kind of commitment.

This one is true, friend. The singer says, "How blessed are those who dwell in Your house! They are ever praising You." (Psalm 84:4). The people who live there are blessed, and the praising just keeps going.

Yes, friend, you got it. The singer says, "Blessed are those whose strength is in You, whose hearts are set on pilgrimage." (Psalm 84:5) The "You" is the LORD, so that's where their strength is. Their strength isn't packed in their bags. It's in the LORD, and that's a good thing to carry on a long road.

Nice guess, but the verse doesn't mention a crowd. It says, "Blessed are those whose strength is in You…" (Psalm 84:5). The "You" is the LORD. Their strength comes from Him, not from how many people are walking.

I get it, money feels like strength on a road trip. But the verse says, "Blessed are those whose strength is in You…" (Psalm 84:5). The "You" is the LORD. Their strength is in Him, not in what's in their pockets.

That's it, friend. "As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs…" (Psalm 84:6). Springs, as in water. The travelers walk through, and the valley comes out of it different. That's a good walk.

Ruins would be a sad ending, and that isn't this song. The verse says, "As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs…" (Psalm 84:6). These travelers leave springs behind them.

Whoa, nobody said anything about a fight. The verse says, "As they pass through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs…" (Psalm 84:6). Springs is the word. The travelers walk through, and the valley changes.

Nope, nobody's turning around. The singer says, "They go from strength to strength, until each appears before God in Zion." (Psalm 84:7). They keep going all the way to the end. No U-turns on this road.

Right, friend. The singer says, "They go from strength to strength, until each appears before God in Zion." (Psalm 84:7) They don't turn back. Each one makes it to Zion and appears before God. No U-turns on this road.

That's the one, friend. "Take notice of our shield, O God, and look with favor on the face of Your anointed." (Psalm 84:9). The singer asks God to look with favor on the face of His anointed. The song doesn't say here who that is, so I'll leave it right there.
Good thought, since this is a song. But the prayer asks God to look with favor on "…the face of Your anointed." (Psalm 84:9). Singers aren't named in that line. It's God's anointed.

Elders are a fair guess in a prayer like this. But the verse says, "Take notice of our shield, O God, and look with favor on the face of Your anointed." (Psalm 84:9). No elders show up in that line. It's God's anointed.
Yes, friend! The singer says, "For better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere." (Psalm 84:10) One day against a thousand, and the one day wins. That's some math I can get behind.

explanations.answer: As good as a week elsewhere
explanations.explanation: A week is generous, but the singer goes way bigger. He says, "For better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere." (Psalm 84:10). A thousand days, and the one day still beats them all.

Not quite, friend. The singer says, "For better is one day in Your courts than a thousand elsewhere." (Psalm 84:10). One day there is better than a thousand days anywhere else. That's a lot more than just the same.

Other way around, friend. He says, "I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked." (Psalm 84:10). He'd take the doorkeeper job in God's house over a home in the tents of the wicked.

Right, friend. The singer says, "I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked." (Psalm 84:10). A doorkeeper is the one at the entrance of God's house. That's the place he says he would rather be.

That's right, friend. "He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity." (Psalm 84:11). The same verse says the LORD God is a sun and a shield, and that He gives grace and glory. That's quite a list.

explanations.answer: Those who bring the most offerings
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd think that, but the verse doesn't say it. It says, "He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity." (Psalm 84:11). It's about how a person walks, not how big the offering is.

explanations.answer: Those who live closest to Zion
explanations.explanation: Zion comes up in this song, so it's a fair guess. But the verse says, "He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity." (Psalm 84:11). It's about how a person walks, not where the house is.

explanations.answer: The man who trusts in the LORD
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. The song ends, "O LORD of Hosts, how blessed is the man who trusts in You!" (Psalm 84:12). After all that longing and walking, the last word is about trust. It's a good place to land.

explanations.answer: The man who serves as priest
explanations.explanation: A priest is a natural guess in a song about God's house. But the last verse says, "O LORD of Hosts, how blessed is the man who trusts in You!" (Psalm 84:12). The blessing goes to the one who trusts.

explanations.answer: The man who builds the altar
explanations.explanation: The altars do get a mention earlier in the song. But the last verse says, "O LORD of Hosts, how blessed is the man who trusts in You!" (Psalm 84:12). The blessed one is the man who trusts in the LORD.
